title: Compact angle spectra and classification
subtitle: G2 lecture 051000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: In finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, the principal angles of two subspaces come from the singular values of their cross-Gram matrix.
body: Together with the dimensions of their common, crossed-perpendicular, and exterior parts, those angles classify the pair up to an orthogonal or unitary change of coordinates. But we are working toward results about Hilbert spaces that may be infinite-dimensional. A bounded self-adjoint operator on an infinite-dimensional space need not have an eigenvector basis. So we should not assume that every pair of subspaces comes with a complete list of principal angles.

slides.title: What exactly are we classifying?
slides.lead: Imagine two ordered pairs of closed subspaces.
body: One pair lives in a Hilbert space H, and the other pair lives in a possibly different Hilbert space G. We will call the pairs equivalent if there is a linear isometric equivalence from H onto G that carries the first source subspace onto the second source subspace and, simultaneously, carries the first target onto the second target. The word simultaneously is essential. It would be easy to match the source spaces separately and the target spaces separately. The challenge is to find one ambient unitary that respects both choices at once. Any such unitary preserves inner products, orthogonality, and projections.

slides.title: The generic cosine block
slides.lead: Focus on the part of the generic space that lies in the source subspace U.
body: On that space consider the operator obtained by projecting into V and then back into U. This is the compression of P U times P V times P U. Call it A. Its quadratic form at a source vector x is the squared length of the projection of x onto V. Therefore A is positive, and it cannot exceed the identity. In finite dimensions, A has eigenvalues cosine squared theta, one for each generic principal angle theta. The common part would give eigenvalue one, and the source defect would give eigenvalue zero, but those endpoint pieces are excluded from the generic summand by construction.

slides.title: Why compactness supplies eigenvectors
slides.lead: Recall what compactness means for a bounded operator: it sends every bounded sequence to a sequence with a convergent subsequence of images.
body: For a positive compact operator A, suppose A is nonzero. Its operator norm equals the maximum possible Rayleigh quotient. Choose unit vectors whose Rayleigh quotients approach that norm. The unit ball of a Hilbert space is weakly sequentially compact. We can choose a weakly convergent subsequence. Compactness upgrades the images under A to strong convergence. This is enough to show that the maximum is attained by a unit vector.

slides.title: The angle list and its multiplicities
slides.lead: Assume the generic cosine operator is compact.
body: Its positive eigenvalues are numbers between zero and one. They represent cosine squared of the generic principal angles. Suppose the same eigenvalue occurs on a three-dimensional eigenspace. That is one angle with multiplicity three. We must record that multiplicity, because three independent principal planes carry more geometric information than one. It is often convenient to record a function: for each possible eigenvalue, give the dimension of its eigenspace. Equivalently, arrange the positive eigenvalues in decreasing order and repeat each according to its multiplicity.

slides.title: A diagonal infinite-dimensional example
slides.lead: Take a Hilbert space of square-summable sequences, with orthonormal basis indexed by the nonnegative integers.
body: Define a cosine operator C that multiplies the coordinate with index n by one over n plus two. Its eigenvalues are one half, one third, one fourth, and so on. The operator is compact, because its finite-coordinate truncations converge to it in operator norm. Now define a sine operator S by taking the positive square root of identity minus C squared. Since C and S are diagonal, they commute, and their squares add to the identity. On a doubled sequence space, take U to be the first coordinate copy. Construct V as the image of the isometric map sending x to the pair C x, S x.

slides.title: A continuous-spectrum example
slides.lead: Now replace the sequence space by the space of square-integrable functions on the interval from zero to one.
body: Let C multiply a function by its input coordinate t. Let S multiply by the square root of one minus t squared. Again, C squared plus S squared is the identity, and both operators are positive and commute. Construct U and V in the doubled function space exactly as before: U is the first copy, and V consists of pairs C f, S f. What are the eigenvectors of C? An eigenvector with eigenvalue lambda would be a nonzero square-integrable function supported where t equals lambda. But a single point has measure zero. So that function must be zero. C has no eigenvectors at all.

slides.title: The compact classification statement
slides.lead: We can now state a useful version of the classification theorem.
body: Consider two ordered pairs of closed subspaces. Suppose, for each pair, the ambient operator P U P V P U is compact. Then the associated generic cosine block is compact as well. The pairs are unitarily equivalent as ordered pairs if and only if their four elementary Halmos summands are isometrically equivalent, and the generic cosine-square eigenvalues have matching multiplicities at every eigenvalue. To see necessity, let an ambient unitary carry one pair to the other. It carries all four elementary pieces, and it intertwines the two cosine-square operators. Intertwining preserves eigenspaces and their dimensions.

slides.title: Reconstruction
slides.lead: First, explain why an ambient equivalence must preserve each of the four elementary Halmos parts.
body: Second, derive positivity of the generic compression of P U P V P U, and interpret each of its eigenvalues as cosine squared of a principal angle. Third, reproduce the compactness argument showing that nonzero eigenvalues have finite multiplicity and can accumulate only at zero. Finally, compare the diagonal sequence example with the multiplication-by-t example. Which one admits a complete numerical list, and why does the other not? We have completed the classification foundations for two subspaces.
